definition: A tool that runs your SQL SELECTs as version-controlled, tested, documented transformation steps (the T in ELT).
explanation: dbt brings software engineering to SQL: each model is a SELECT dbt materializes as a view/table, with dependencies, tests, docs, and CI. It handles the transform layer inside the warehouse, not ingestion or orchestration.
interviewLine: dbt runs SQL SELECTs as tested, version-controlled models inside the warehouse — the T of ELT with engineering rigor.
whyItMatters: dbt is the de-facto standard for the transformation layer of the modern data stack.
interviewQuestion: Why did dbt push the industry from ETL toward ELT?

definition: A model is a single .sql file containing one SELECT; dbt turns it into a table or view in the warehouse.
explanation: You write business logic as a SELECT and dbt wraps it in the right DDL. Models are layered by convention: staging (clean sources) → intermediate (reusable logic) → marts (business-facing facts/dims).
interviewLine: A dbt model is one SELECT dbt materializes; teams layer them staging → intermediate → marts for clarity and reuse.
whyItMatters: Modeling in layers keeps transformations readable, testable, and reusable across a team.

example.content:
-- models/marts/orders.sql
select
  o.order_id,
  o.customer_id,
  sum(oi.amount) as order_total
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }} o
join {{ ref('stg_order_items') }} oi using (order_id)
group by 1, 2

definition: A declared reference to a raw table loaded into the warehouse, used via source() and freshness-checked.
explanation: You define sources in YAML (schema + table), then read them with {{ source('jaffle','orders') }}. This documents raw inputs, lets dbt test their freshness, and draws the lineage back to where data landed.
interviewLine: Sources declare raw loaded tables so dbt can reference them, test freshness, and root lineage at the ingestion boundary.
whyItMatters: Sources make the boundary between 'raw loaded data' and 'dbt-owned models' explicit and testable.

definition: ref() links one model to another; dbt reads those links to build a DAG and run models in dependency order.
explanation: Never hard-code table names — use {{ ref('stg_orders') }}. dbt parses every ref() into a dependency graph, then runs models in topological order, parallelizing independent branches. That graph is also your lineage.
interviewLine: ref() declares model dependencies; dbt compiles them into a DAG to order and parallelize runs and to render lineage.
whyItMatters: ref() is what makes dbt a build system: correct ordering, parallelism, and free lineage.
commonMistake: Hard-coding a table name instead of ref() — dbt then can't order the build or track lineage.

definition: How dbt persists a model: view, table, incremental, or ephemeral — a per-model performance/cost choice.
explanation: view: no storage, always fresh, recomputed on read. table: rebuilt fully each run, fast reads. incremental: only process new rows. ephemeral: inlined as a CTE, no object. You pick per model by size and freshness needs.
interviewLine: Materializations decide how a model is stored — view, table, incremental, ephemeral — trading build cost against read speed.
whyItMatters: Choosing materializations is the main way you tune dbt build time and warehouse cost.
interviewQuestion: When would you switch a model from table to incremental?

definition: A materialization that processes only new/changed rows each run instead of rebuilding the whole table.
explanation: You add an is_incremental() filter (e.g. where updated_at > max in the table) and a unique_key for upserts. dbt builds the table once, then appends/merges deltas — essential for billion-row event tables.
interviewLine: Incremental models filter to new rows via is_incremental() and a unique_key, so big tables update in minutes, not full rebuilds.
whyItMatters: Incremental is how dbt stays affordable on huge, ever-growing tables.
commonMistake: Forgetting late-arriving data — a naive max(updated_at) filter silently drops rows that arrive out of order.

definition: Assertions on your data: generic tests (unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships) and custom singular tests.
explanation: Generic tests are declared in YAML on a column (unique, not_null, foreign-key relationships). Singular tests are a SQL query that should return zero rows. dbt test runs them; CI blocks a merge if data fails.
interviewLine: dbt tests assert data quality — generic ones (unique, not_null, relationships) plus singular SQL tests — and gate the build in CI.
whyItMatters: Tests turn silent data corruption into a failing build before bad data reaches dashboards.
interviewQuestion: How do dbt tests fit into a CI pipeline on a pull request?

definition: dbt's built-in way to capture SCD Type 2 history of a mutable source table over time.
explanation: Point a snapshot at a source with a unique key and a strategy (timestamp or check columns). On each run dbt detects changes and writes new versioned rows with dbt_valid_from/to — SCD Type 2 without hand-writing it.
interviewLine: Snapshots record SCD Type 2 history: dbt versions changed rows with valid-from/to columns using a timestamp or check strategy.
whyItMatters: It gives you dimension history for free — a task teams otherwise build by hand and get wrong.

definition: Small static CSV files, version-controlled in the repo, that dbt loads into the warehouse as tables.
explanation: dbt seed loads a CSV (country codes, mappings, thresholds) into a table you can ref() like any model. Best for small, rarely-changing lookup data that belongs in version control — not for bulk data loading.
interviewLine: Seeds are version-controlled CSVs dbt loads as tables — ideal for small lookup data, not for bulk ingestion.
whyItMatters: Seeds keep reference data reviewed and versioned alongside the models that use it.
commonMistake: Using seeds to load large or frequently-changing data — that's an ingestion tool's job, not dbt's.

definition: dbt compiles SQL through Jinja templating; macros are reusable functions that generate SQL.
explanation: Jinja gives you variables, loops, and conditionals inside SQL (that's how ref() and is_incremental() work). A macro packages repeated logic — e.g. cents_to_dollars() or a loop that pivots columns — into one callable function.
interviewLine: dbt templates SQL with Jinja; macros are reusable functions that generate SQL, keeping repeated logic DRY.
whyItMatters: Macros are how teams keep transformation logic DRY instead of copy-pasting SQL.

definition: Shareable bundles of dbt models, macros, and tests you import into your project via packages.yml.
explanation: Packages like dbt_utils, dbt_expectations, and codegen give you battle-tested macros and generic tests. You add them to packages.yml and dbt deps installs them — reuse instead of reinventing common utilities.
interviewLine: Packages import shared models/macros/tests (like dbt_utils) via packages.yml, so teams reuse proven utilities.
whyItMatters: Packages save teams from re-writing surrogate-key, pivot, and test-suite logic everyone needs.

definition: dbt generates a browsable docs site with model descriptions, column info, and an interactive DAG.
explanation: dbt docs generate builds a site from your YAML descriptions and the ref() graph, including a clickable lineage diagram showing how each model flows from sources to marts. It's living documentation that can't drift.
interviewLine: dbt auto-generates docs and an interactive lineage DAG from ref() and YAML, so documentation stays in sync with the code.
whyItMatters: Auto-generated lineage answers 'what breaks if I change this?' without tribal knowledge.

definition: A declared downstream consumer of your models (a dashboard, app, or ML pipeline) tracked in the lineage graph.
explanation: An exposure names a real consumer in YAML and lists the models it depends on. Now lineage extends past the warehouse — you can see which dashboards a model feeds and run/test only what a given exposure needs.
interviewLine: Exposures declare downstream consumers (dashboards, apps) in the DAG, extending lineage to real-world impact of a change.
whyItMatters: Exposures close the lineage loop, showing the real-world impact of a model change.

definition: dbt transforms data inside the warehouse; Airflow orchestrates when and in what order jobs (including dbt) run.
explanation: They're complementary, not rivals. dbt owns the SQL transformation DAG and tests. Airflow (or Dagster) schedules pipelines: ingest → run dbt → trigger downstream. A common pattern is Airflow invoking dbt as one task.
interviewLine: dbt is the in-warehouse transform layer; Airflow is the orchestrator that schedules it alongside ingestion and downstream jobs.
whyItMatters: Confusing the two is a common junior mistake; naming the split signals real stack understanding.
commonMistake: Treating dbt as a scheduler — dbt builds models; something else must decide when to run it.
